sections.text: This checkpoint practises Unit 5: vectors, String and &str, and HashMap. You will write three functions that split a text into words and count them.
It draws on the lessons Vectors, String and &str and HashMap. HashMap<String, u32> is a map with String keys and u32 values, in the same way as Vec<String> is a list of Strings.

todo!() is a placeholder. If the program reaches it, it stops with the message "not yet implemented". Replace each todo!() with your own code. Until you do, the compiler may warn that some names are unused. That is expected.

Hint for split_words: make an empty vector with let mut words = Vec::new();. Then loop over text.split_whitespace(). It gives the words as &str and ignores extra spaces. word.to_lowercase() makes a new String, which you can push onto the vector.

Hint for word_counts: a HashMap owns its keys, so each key must be a String. In the loop, word is a &String, so give word.clone() to entry. Then use or_insert(0) and add 1, as in the HashMap lesson. The last line gives back the map.
Hint for count_of: get returns an Option that holds a reference to the number. Use unwrap_or(&0) for a missing word, and * to get the number out. get accepts a &str even though the keys are Strings.
A HashMap does not keep its keys in a fixed order. That is why main sorts the keys before it prints them.

exercise.prompt:
Replace each todo!() with working code. Do not change main.

fn split_words(text: &str) -> Vec<String>
Gives back the words of text, in order, each one in lowercase. Words are separated by whitespace (spaces, tabs or new lines), and extra whitespace is ignored. Punctuation stays part of the word. A text with no words gives an empty Vec.

fn word_counts(words: &[String]) -> HashMap<String, u32>
Gives back a map from each different word to the number of times it appears. It uses the words exactly as given and does not change their case.

fn count_of(counts: &HashMap<String, u32>, word: &str) -> u32
Gives back how many times word appears in counts, or 0 if it is not there. It looks up word exactly as given.

When the functions work, main prints:
8 words
and: 2
cat: 1
end: 1
hat: 1
the: 3
the appears 3 times
dog appears 0 times
[spaced]
[out]
0 words, 0 different

tests.label: split_words lowercases every word
tests.code: check_eq!(split_words("The cat and THE end"), vec!["the", "cat", "and", "the", "end"]);

tests.label: split_words gives an empty Vec for empty text
word_counts counts how often each word appears
count_of gives the count of a word in the map
count_of gives 0 for a missing word
Tabs and new lines separate words too
Text with only whitespace has no words
Punctuation stays part of the word
tests.code:
check_eq!(split_words("Hello, World!"), vec!["hello,", "world!"]);
check_eq!(split_words("it's a-b"), vec!["it's", "a-b"]);

tests.label: Words stay in order and repeats are kept
tests.code:
check_eq!(split_words("b a b A"), vec!["b", "a", "b", "a"]);
check_eq!(split_words("go go stop"), vec!["go", "go", "stop"]);

tests.label: No words gives an empty map
One word repeated many times
word_counts does not change case
Each different word gets 1
count_of on an empty map gives 0
count_of looks up the word exactly as given
count_of with several words in the map
The two functions work together

hints: split_words builds a Vec in a loop over split_whitespace(), and to_lowercase() makes each new String. word_counts fills a HashMap with entry and or_insert. count_of uses get, which gives an Option because the word may be missing.
A HashMap owns its keys, so give entry a String: word.clone(). Add 1 to the value that or_insert(0) gives back. In count_of, unwrap_or(&0) gives a reference, so put a * in front to get the number.
In word_counts, the loop body is *counts.entry(word.clone()).or_insert(0) += 1; and the last line is counts. In count_of, the whole body is *counts.get(word).unwrap_or(&0).

quiz.question: Why does word_counts give word.clone() to entry?
options: clone is needed for every HashMap call
The map owns its keys, but word is only a borrowed reference
quiz.explanation: The HashMap owns its keys, so entry needs an owned String. Here word is only a reference to a String inside the slice, and word.clone() makes the owned copy the map can keep. Not every HashMap call needs a clone, and keys can be any type that can be hashed.

quiz.question: What does len() count for a String?
quiz.explanation: len() on a String counts bytes, not characters or words. For plain English letters one byte is one character, but characters such as é take more than one byte. Use chars().count() to count characters.

quiz.question: What does counts.get("dog") return when "dog" is not in the map?
quiz.explanation: get never panics: it returns an Option, and a missing key gives None. It doesn't give 0, because 0 could be a real count. Indexing with counts["dog"] is the form that panics for a missing key.
